exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 41 and 42 reveal an important connection between linear independence and linear transformations and provide practice using the definition of linear dependence. Let $$V$$ and $$W$$ be vector spaces, let $$\left. T:V\rightarrow W \right.$$ be a linear transformation, and let $$\text{\{} \mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ be a subset of $$V$$ .

problem.paragraph: Show that if $$\text{\{} \mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ is linearly dependent in $$V$$ , then the set of images, $$\text{\{} T(\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{)} ,\ldots,T(\mathbf{v}_{p} \text{)\}}$$ , is linearly dependent in $$W$$ . This fact shows that if a linear transformation maps a set $$\text{\{} \mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ onto a linearly independent set $$\text{\{} T(\mathbf{v}_{1}),\ldots,T(\mathbf{v}_{p} \text{)\}}$$ , then the original set is linearly independent, too (because it cannot be linearly dependent).

Suppose that $$T$$ is a one-to-one transformation, so that an equation $$T\left( \mathbf{u} \right) = T\left( \mathbf{v} \right)$$ always implies $$\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$$ . Show that if the set of images $$\text{\{} T(\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{)} ,\ldots,T(\mathbf{v}_{p} \text{)\}}$$ is linearly dependent, then $$\text{\{} \mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ is linearly dependent. This fact shows that a one-to-one linear transformation maps a linearly independent set onto a linearly independent set (because in this case the set of images cannot be linearly dependent).

problem.paragraph: [T] Show that $$\left\{ {1,\cos t,\cos^{2}t,\ldots,\cos^{6}t} \right\}$$ is a linearly independent set of functions defined on $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Use the method of Exercise 47. (This result will be needed in Exercise 54 in Section 4.5.)

Let $$A = \lbrack\begin{matrix} \mathbf{v}_{1} & \mathbf{v}_{2} \end{matrix}\rbrack$$ . Row operations show that $$A = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & - 2 \\ - 2 & 7 \\ 3 & 9\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Not every row of $$A$$ contains a pivot position. So the columns of $$A$$ do not span $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ , by Theorem 4 in Section 1.4. Hence $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ is not a basis for $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ . Since $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ are not in $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ , they cannot possibly be a basis for $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ . However, since $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ are obviously linearly independent, they are a basis for a subspace of $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ , namely $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ .

Set up a matrix $$A$$ whose column space is the space spanned by $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{4} \right\}$$ , and then row reduce $$A$$ to find its pivot columns. $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 & 2 & - 4 \\ - 3 & 2 & - 2 & - 8 \\ 4 & - 1 & 3 & 9 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 & 2 & - 4 \\ 0 & 20 & 4 & - 20 \\ 0 & - 25 & - 5 & 25 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 & 2 & - 4 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 & - 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

The first two columns of $$A$$ are the pivot columns and hence form a basis of $$A = W$$ . Hence $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ is a basis for $$W$$ . Note that the reduced echelon form of $$A$$ is not needed in order to locate the pivot columns.

Neither $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ nor $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ is in $$H$$ , so $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ cannot be a basis for $$H$$ . In fact, $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ is a basis for the plane of all vectors of the form $$(c_{1} \text{,} c_{2} \text{,} 0)$$ , but $$H$$ is only a line.

Since $$\text{\{} \mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ is a basis for $$V$$ , for any vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ , there exist scalars $$c_{1}, \text{…} ,c_{p}$$ such that $$\mathbf{x} = c_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\mathbf{v}_{p}$$ . Then since $$T$$ and $$U$$ are linear transformations $$T \left(\mathbf{x}\right) & = & T ( c_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{v}_{p} ) = c_{1} T \left(\mathbf{v}_{1}\right) + \hdots + c_{p} T ( \mathbf{v}_{p} ) & = & c_{1} U \left(\mathbf{v}_{1}\right) + \hdots + c_{p} U ( \mathbf{v}_{p} ) = U ( c_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{v}_{p} ) & = & U \left(\mathbf{x}\right)$$
